newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin lashes corruption, graft, urges reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin lashes corruption, graft, urges reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday lashed out at corruption as a threat to the security of Russia and said he was sure his government would win the age-old battle against graft.
He admitted that the task would not be easy. "I know that you will nevertheless have your doubts about our victory over corruption," he said in a radio address to the Russian people.
"But I am determined, I have the political will and I have your backing in this fight. I will bring this difficult struggle to an end. It will become scary to steal and to take bribes."
Yeltsin, 66, said Russia needed to create an authoritative and efficient state power.

"Corruption is one of the main reasons that the authority of the Russian state is low today," he said. "This is preventing us from bringing order to the country and threatening the very security of Russia."
Yeltsin said major reforms were needed to eliminate graft, a tough task for his newly reshuffled cabinet.

"Punitive measures will not reverse the situation, a renewal of power is needed, a reform of the whole system of state management. These tasks may be fulfilled by young people. They have the strength and we can demand more from them. Such people are already in the government," Yeltsin said.
He said Russia had to prevent the theft and expropriation of state assets, and that this would free up more money for payments of social benefits, wages and pensions.
"The most reliable barrier against corruption must be put first of all within the treasury, in the whole system of state finances," he said.
Yeltsin said Russia would introduce open tenders for state purchases from May 1 in order to reduce the possibility of wrongdoing by state officials.
"This will eliminate a loophole, will cut wrongdoing by officials drastically," Yeltsin said, adding that the bureacracy had to be prevented from growing further.

Yeltsin, who has returned resolutely to the political fray after eight months absence with heart problems and pneumonia, has adopted radio addresses as his favourite mode of addressing the Russian people.
He said he was preparing a decree ordering officials and their families to declare their income and assets.

"A state official is, above all, a civilian officer, an example of honour and dignity for society," Yeltsin said, adding that he had ordered a list of ethical rules for officials and a State Service Code to be drawn up by November 1.
